name: November 3, 2026 General Election
eyebrow: November 3, 2026 · California · Santa Clara County · San José
lede: The 14 statewide measures plus the local measures on San José ballots, explained from the official Voter Information Guide and the Legislative Analyst's nonpartisan analysis. Each side's case is shown in its own words. This guide makes no recommendations.

keyDates.label: OCT 27
keyDates.text: Last day to request a new mail ballot

keyDates.label: NOV 3
keyDates.text: Election Day · polls 7 a.m.–8 p.m. · mail ballots must be postmarked by today

keyDates.label: NOV 10
keyDates.text: Last day for postmarked mail ballots to arrive

jurisdictions.title: 14 statewide propositions
jurisdictions.intro: Select a measure for what a Yes or No vote does, the fiscal impact, both sides' arguments, and the money behind each side. Measures marked Linked interact with others on this ballot. Every statewide measure passes with a simple majority.

jurisdictions.title: Local measures
jurisdictions.intro: A San José ballot this November has the 14 state propositions, the regional transit tax (RTM), and, depending on your address, a school district measure.
notOnBallot: No City of San José measures on November 3. The city's only 2026 measure, Measure A (hotel tax from 4% to 6%, about $10M a year for general city services), was decided June 2 and led with about 66% in early returns.

No countywide Santa Clara County measures. Other cities in the county have their own measures (Palo Alto, Mountain View, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Santa Clara, Cupertino, Gilroy, Morgan Hill, Los Altos), which San José voters do not see.

sections.title: Depends on your school district
sections.note: Your sample ballot booklet lists exactly which measures you'll see. You can also look up your ballot at VOTE411.

jurisdictions.method: Local measures have no LAO analysis. Their facts come from the measure's ballot question, district materials, and named secondary sources, and the official arguments are in the Santa Clara County voter information guide. Campaign money for local measures is not compiled yet.

money.intro: Reported contributions from top donors to committees supporting and opposing each measure. Committees reported about $636 million across 11 measures as of October 5. The billionaire tax fight (Props 40–42) accounts for more than a third.
money.source: Source: FPPC Top 10 Contributors lists as of October 5, 2026, as compiled by California Today (Oct 19 update). Figures change weekly; totals cover top contributors only. Where a "No" bar is empty, no opposing committee reported $1M or more, or opposition runs through another measure's committee (41 and 42 are opposed by the Yes on 40 campaign).
funders: ~$262M total: No on 40 ($88.5M), Yes on 42 ($97.8M), Yes on 41 ($58.35M), Yes on 45 ($10M), Yes on 37 ($6M), Yes on 1 ($1M). The FPPC lists its top donors as Sergey Brin and John Doerr.
~$49M: Yes on 40 ($31.8M), Yes on 44 ($16.9M). Also the listed opponent of 41 and 42.
